summary: David asks God to reveal when he will die, and though God refuses to reveal the exact date, He reveals that David will die on a Shabbat.
A sage would seek out pairs of scholars talking on Shabbat and exhort them to ensure they were properly delighting in the day.
It narrates a specific conflict between Rav's public announcement and Rav Amram Ḥasida's physical enforcement (lashes), involving different actors and a distinct outcome from the subsequent story.
The Rabbis report to Rav Ashi that Rav Huna used a piece of garlic as a makeshift plug/filter, and Rav Ashi defends the practice as a permissible form of artifice for a scholar.
The mothers and wives of sages prepare mustard on Shabbat, but their students/sons refuse to eat it, leading to a confrontation about their stringency.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta why he did not visit during the festival, and Shimon explains how the physical toll of old age has made the journey impossible.
An apostate challenges Rabbi Abbahu regarding the location of souls and the biblical story of Samuel and the necromancer.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recounts how his family once celebrated their traditional festival when it coincided with the Ninth of Av, choosing not to complete the fast.
A group of Sages travel from Pelandarsin by boat and find themselves at sea as Shabbat begins.
Neḥemya son of Rav Ḥanilai accidentally wanders outside the Shabbat limit while studying, and Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Naḥman to arrange a human partition to bring him back.
A Galilean woman's attempt to invite her friend for milk results in a garbled, nonsensical sentence due to her accent.

Passage B describes a distinct, recurring habit of Rabbi Abbahu using enigmatic language in a domestic setting, whereas Passage A is a specific dialogue between the Sages and Rabbi Abbahu regarding Rabbi Elai.

Passage B is a distinct narrative incident involving Rabbi Elai and a group of questioners, featuring a specific verbal exchange and a clever metaphorical response, which is independent of Rabbi Yehoshua's story in Passage A.
While sitting with his teacher, Ravina sees a man violating a law and shouts to stop him, later receiving his teacher's approval for acting in his presence to prevent a sin.
Mar Shmuel permitted his household to use a large mortar to secure a door on Shabbat.
Three priests describe their small portions of showbread, and the one who uses a crude metaphor is investigated and found to be disqualified from service.

Passage B describes a specific historical debate between Baitos ben Zonin and the Sages involving a concrete proposal (using a mold) and a definitive rejection, distinct from the father-son dialogue in Passage A.
Rabbi Yehoshua married a priest's daughter, fell ill, and attributed his illness to Aaron's displeasure with the match.
The residents of Ḥozai report their custom of separating challah from rice to Rav Yosef, who orders a public violation of the custom to correct them, leading to a legal challenge by Abaye.
Jacob attempts to reveal the end of days to his sons but loses his prophetic inspiration, leading to a dialogue about their faith and the origin of a liturgical response.
When God decrees that Adam will eat the herb of the field, Adam weeps and pleads not to be equated with his donkey.
Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna visit the Exilarch and are lodged by Rav Nahman in a sukkah they would normally consider unfit, yet they remain silent.
Rabbi Yehuda begins to cite an incident regarding the four species.
Two heretics named Sason and Simḥa debate their relative importance using biblical verses, ending in Simḥa's witty put-down.
A heretic named Sason mocks Rabbi Abbahu regarding the afterlife, but the Rabbi uses a grammatical nuance to prove the heretic will be the one serving.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok describes how young priests would descend into a gap by the altar every seventy years to collect congealed wine residue.
Levi performs a difficult prostration before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and is injured, becoming lame.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava rebukes Shimon the Timnite for missing the study hall on a Festival to protect his property from soldiers.
Ameimar has his eye treated by a gentile on Shabbat, and Rav Ashi argues that Ameimar's blinking constitutes prohibited assistance in the act.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends a firstborn animal to Rabbi Ami for examination on a festival, but Rabbi Ami is stopped from doing so by an objection from Rabbi Zerika.
Rav and Shmuel, who avoided a dilapidated wall for thirteen years, finally walk past it when the meritorious Rav Adda bar Ahava is with them.
When a plague skips Rav's neighborhood, a dream reveals it is due to the merit of a man who lends tools for burials rather than Rav's own merit.
A fire in Drokart avoids Rav Huna's neighborhood, and a dream reveals this was due to the merit of a woman who shared her oven.
Passage B is a complete narrative about Rabbi Yona's humble method of praying for rain, distinct from the narrative in Passage A regarding his son Rabbi Mani's persecution by the house of the Nasi.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decrees a fast for rain that fails, leading him to lament his generation's spiritual standing compared to the prophet Samuel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish are informed of a fast too late to accept it properly, but decide to observe it regardless.
When Rabbi's fast fails to bring rain, Ilfa leads the prayer and the wind and rain respond immediately to his words.
Rav encounters a prayer leader whose prayer brings rain because of his selfless devotion to teaching the children of the poor.
Rabba discusses why his generation's prayers are not answered compared to Rav Yehuda's generation, despite their superior Torah study.
When rain falls early during a fast decreed by Shmuel HaKatan, he tells a parable to explain that God granted the rain quickly only to stop hearing their voices.
On another occasion, rain falls after sunset following a fast, and Shmuel HaKatan again rebukes the people's assumption that this indicates their merit.
Abraham expresses concern to God about Israel's survival after the Temple's destruction, leading God to establish the reading of the sacrificial order as a means of atonement.
Joshua encounters an angel who rebukes the people for neglecting Torah study and sacrifices.

The Gemara expands on the Megillah narrative, detailing how Haman was forced to personally groom Mordecai and serve as his mounting block, leading to his public humiliation and the death of his daughter.
After Rabbi Hiyya insults Rabbi Shimon's voice, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells his son to point out Rabbi Hiyya's own inability to pronounce certain letters correctly.
A baraita records that Rabbi Zakkai inherited 300 barrels of wine from his mother and left 3,000 to his sons, attributed to his piety.
Passage B is a distinct narrative incident involving Reish Lakish and a specific scholar, serving as a thematic foil to the subsequent story about Rav Nachman in Passage A.
When a man who had memorized many texts died, Rav Nachman refused to eulogize him, arguing that he was merely a container for books rather than a true scholar.
Mar Ukva, distracted by a legal case, fails to honor Shmuel as usual, leading Shmuel to rebuke him in a way that the Gemara defines as a one-day admonition.
An incident is recounted where a leading sage refrained from removing his garment in mourning for his father because another sage intended to do the same out of respect.
Abaye observes Rav Yosef practicing mourning rites privately on Shabbat and questions him about the legality of the act.
At Rav Hisda's funeral, Rabbi Yitzhak prevented the Sages from placing a Torah on the bier and provided instructions on when to sew their mourning tears.
Passage B describes a distinct event involving the death and eulogy of Rabbi Zeira, featuring different actors and a different narrative focus than the mourning of Rabbi Yoḥanan in Passage A.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Ḥisma visit Rabbi Yehoshua and recount the homilies delivered by Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya in the study hall.
Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed to learn proper conduct, but his presence is discovered when he makes a comment about Rav's behavior.
An elderly Rabbi Ya’akov refuses his teacher's suggestion to stop his daily visits, arguing that seeing sages brings life.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei seeks dissolution for a vow after an incident where a launderer hit him.
A midrashic expansion of the biblical account where angels swallow Moses for neglecting circumcision until Zipporah intervenes.
Abraham trembles when commanded to be wholehearted, and God takes him outside to show him he is above the stars.
Miriam prophesies the birth of a savior, and when Moses is born and fills the house with light, her father kisses her in recognition.
Kings who came to fight the family of Jacob changed their minds upon seeing Joseph's crown on Jacob's casket and hung their own crowns there in honor.
When Esau prevents Jacob's burial at the Cave of Machpelah, the deaf Hushim, frustrated by the delay, kills Esau, allowing the burial to proceed.
While the Israelites were busy with loot, Moses sought out Serah daughter of Asher to find Joseph's coffin and miraculously caused it to float to the surface of the Nile.
Passage B describes a distinct behavioral change in Rabbi Abbahu regarding liturgical practice, whereas Passage A describes a distinct realization regarding his character trait of humility.
Rabbi Abbahu declines the headship of the yeshiva in favor of the impoverished Rabbi Abba of Akko.
The biblical story of Elisha being taunted by youths and the subsequent bear attack.
A man built a mansion on land belonging to orphans, and Rav Nahman confiscated the building from him.
A man cut down another's date palm and was brought before the Exilarch, who ordered him to pay one hundred zuz based on his own knowledge of the tree's value.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi pull Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa in different directions regarding his teaching, leading him to compare himself to a man with two wives who pluck out all his hair.
Rabbi Yishmael recounts how his family's wealth in the Galilee was lost because they grazed animals improperly and judged cases individually.
An unmarried woman impulsively swears to marry anyone who will discipline her son, but the Sages intervene to dissolve the oath when unworthy men try to hold her to it.

While walking, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya observe Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa refusing to veer off the road; Rabbi Hiyya explains his student's pious motivations, leading to a respectful encounter.
An incident involving a woman's eligibility for marriage comes before the sages, resulting in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitting her to marry a priest.
Avuh bar Ihi bought a loft from his sister, but after a creditor seized it, Shmuel ruled he could not recover his money because no property guarantee was written.
Shabbtai son of Rabbi Marinus pledged a wool cloak to his daughter-in-law but denied it when her marriage contract was lost, only to be contradicted by witnesses.
A man selling silk strips sets a price, and a buyer calculates whether the price constitutes exploitation.
A man selling jewelry sets a price, and a buyer calculates the exploitation involved.

Passage B features a distinct set of actors (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yishmael) and a specific dialogue-based encounter that evaluates the preceding events, constituting a separate narrative unit.
Rabba initially refused to sit on synagogue mats bought with charity funds until he learned that the townspeople have the right to change the designation of such funds.
The Gemara recounts the historical evolution of the Jewish school system, culminating in Yehoshua ben Gamla's decree to establish local schools to prevent the loss of Torah knowledge.
Rabbi Oshaya disagrees with his father Rabbi Hama on a ruling and consults his grandfather Rabbi Bisa, leading Rami bar Hama to praise the three generations of scholars.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rav Safra describe sightings of fantastic sea creatures while traveling by ship.
A man known for his many debts publicly admits to owing specific people, but Rav Nachman rules the admission invalid as it may have been a lie to hide his wealth.
The Sages of Tiberias send a letter to Mar Ukva regarding a complaint brought by Ukvan against his brother Yirmeya.
After Rabbi Sheila publicly lectured that Joshua was personally sinful, Rav waited for him to leave and then appointed an interpreter to teach the public that Joshua was actually blameless.
The Gemara relates how Hezekiah's mother saved him from his father's attempt to sacrifice him to an idol by rubbing him with fireproof salamander blood.
A woman tries to collect dust from under Rabbi Hanina's feet for sorcery, but he tells her to proceed if she can, as he trusts in God's exclusive power.
Geviha ben Pesisa engages in a sharp verbal exchange with a heretic who mocks the belief in resurrection.
When Jacob attempts to leave after praying, God causes the sun to set prematurely so that the righteous man will stay at His 'inn' for the night.
After Rabbi Yosei teaches the methods of theft used in Sodom, thieves in Tzippori immediately use those methods, leading the townspeople to blame the Rabbi.
A woman repeatedly brings sets of witnesses who are proven to be liars until Reish Lakish rules that she has established a presumptive status of dishonesty.
A debtor denies a loan existed, but the creditor's witnesses testify that the loan was made and already repaid, leading Abaye to rule on the debtor's status.
A creditor presents a note, the debtor claims payment, and the creditor's admission of receiving money (even if for a different debt) leads Rav Nachman to rule the note is undermined.
A gentile stops a wine leak by placing his hand over the hole, leading Rav Pappa to rule that only the wine directly adjacent to the hand is prohibited.
King Josiah, fearing the prophecy of exile, commands that the Ark and other sacred vessels be hidden away.
When the academy needed a head, Rav Yosef and Rabba sought guidance from Eretz Yisrael, but Rav Yosef ultimately declined the position for twenty-two years.
A group of four sages held a competition to see whose legal reasoning could not be refuted, resulting in Abaye being appointed their leader.

Passage B features a different set of actors (Rav Aha and Rav Ashi) and a different proposed solution (sewing vs. tying) to the same legal problem, following the common Talmudic pattern of grouping similar incidents.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perahya remarks on how his attitude toward holding high office changed once he attained it.
Rav Dimi bar Yitzḥak asks Rabbi Yehuda for a physical demonstration of a spinal boundary; after Rav Dimi brings a kid for the purpose, Rabbi Yehuda decides to teach him the verbal tradition instead.
When Rava is about to declare an animal non-kosher because test perforations don't match, his son Rav Mesharshiyya rubs the tissue until they match, leading to a kosher ruling.
Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok travel to Lod and stop in Ono, where they issue a legal ruling.
Passage B describes a specific event involving a ewe in a neighborhood and a medical intervention, which prompts a response from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, distinct from the hen incidents in Passage A.
On the eve of Yom Kippur, ravens drop meat, and Rav Kahana permits Rav Nahman to eat it.
Passage B is a distinct narrative involving Rabbi Elazar, Ze'eiri, and Rav Yitzḥak bar Avudimi investigating the origins of Rav's ruling, whereas Passage A is the actual event of Rav in Tatlefush.

Rav Dimi's intent to write a legal letter to Rav Yosef leads to a discussion on the prohibition of writing the Oral Law, resolved by the precedent of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish using written Aggada books.
